title: Sense-checking answers: estimate first, plausible tablets, volumes and rates
blurb: Estimate every answer before calculating and spot tenfold, unit and upside-down errors before you type.
question: A calculation gives 25 tablets for a single dose. What has probably gone wrong, and how do you check?

teach.body: Rule: before keying, predict roughly what the answer should be; after keying, compare. If the two disagree by a factor of 10 or more, or the answer is outside a normal range for that item, the calculation has probably slipped somewhere: recheck it. Plain English: a quick guess catches the big slips (decimal point, upside-down fraction, unconverted unit) that cost the mark and, in practice, harm people.

teach.h: Usual sizes of Part A answers
head: Item
Usual range
Recheck if
teach.caption: Typical Part A answer sizes, not clinical limits: an answer outside them is a cue to recheck, not proof of an error (one practice paper keyed 6 tablets).

teach.h: Worked example: Aisha on a children's ward
teach.body: Aisha, a staff nurse, needs 90 mg of a medicine from a suspension of 250 mg/5 mL. Estimate: 90 is a bit over a third of 250, so the volume is a bit over a third of 5 mL, about 2 mL. Calculate: 90 ÷ 250 × 5 = 1.8 mL. The estimate and answer agree, so she moves on.

teach.h: What the classic slips look like

teach.body: 1. Bigger or smaller? If you want more than the stock strength, the answer is more than one tablet or more than the stock volume. 2. Right size? Compare with the usual range. 3. Right unit? A rate should be in mL per hour, a dose volume in mL, a count in tablets or ampoules.

teach.text: The tenfold error: a slipped decimal point turns 1.5 mL into 15 mL or 0.15 mL, and an upside-down fraction turns 3 mL into 1.33 mL. An answer like 25 tablets for one dose or 0.008 mL per hour is a signal to recalculate, not to type.

items: Want more than stock strength: answer bigger than one tablet or the stock volume.
Usual sizes: tablets 0.5–4, liquids up to 30 mL, injections up to 5 mL, pumps 5–500 mL/hour.
A tenfold gap means a decimal, unit or fraction slip.
Recalculate rather than type a surprising answer.

summary: You can now estimate an answer before calculating and compare it with the usual size of tablets, volumes and rates in Part A. You can also recognise the tenfold, unit and inverted-fraction slips and recalculate.

A.q: You have a prescription for 1.5 g. The tablets contain 500 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
A.why: 1.5 g = 1500 mg. 1500 ÷ 500 = 3 tablets. Estimate: three times the tablet strength, so 3.

whyNot.0: Did not convert 1.5 g to 1500 mg.
whyNot.1: Decimal slip: ten times too many.

A.q: You have a prescription for 150 mg. The ampoule label reads 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
A.why: 150 ÷ 100 × 2 = 3 mL. Estimate: 1.5 times the 100 mg, so 1.5 × 2 mL.

whyNot.1: Decimal slip: 30 mL is far too much for one injection.
whyNot.2: Inverted the fraction; you want more than 100 mg, so more than 2 mL.
whyNot.3: Decimal slip: ten times too little.

A.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 2 L, IV, over 16 hours. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
A.why: 2 L = 2000 mL. 2000 ÷ 16 = 125 mL per hour. Estimate: 2000 over about 16 is a bit over 100.

whyNot.1: Decimal slip: ten times too fast.
whyNot.3: Divided the time by the volume in litres (16 ÷ 2).

B.q: A person weighing 82 kg is prescribed 0.05 mg/kg of a medicine. The ampoule label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
B.why: Dose = 82 × 0.05 = 4.1 mg. Volume = 4.1 ÷ 10 = 0.41 mL. Estimate: about 4 mg from 10 mg/mL is under half a mL.

whyNot.0: This is the dose in mg (4.1), not the volume.
whyNot.2: Decimal slip: ten times too small.

B.q: You have a prescription for 12.5 mg. The oral solution label reads 5 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: 12.5 ÷ 5 × 5 = 12.5 mL. Estimate: 5 mg is in 5 mL, so 1 mg per mL.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume (12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5).
whyNot.1: Decimal slip: ten times too little.

B.q: You have a prescription for 0.125 mg. The tablets contain 62.5 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.1: Did not convert mg to micrograms.
whyNot.2: Decimal slip: ten times too many.

C.q: A person weighing 70 kg needs maintenance fluid of 30 mL/kg/day, given evenly by pump over 24 hours. At what rate should the pump be set? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
C.why: Daily = 70 × 30 = 2100 mL. 2100 ÷ 24 = 87.5, so 88 mL per hour. Estimate: about 2000 over 24 is about 80 to 90.

whyNot.0: This is the daily volume, not the hourly rate.
whyNot.1: Decimal slip: ten times too slow.
whyNot.2: Decimal slip: ten times too fast.

C.q: A child weighing 18 kg is prescribed 15 mg/kg of a medicine. The oral suspension label reads 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
C.why: Dose = 18 × 15 = 270 mg. 270 ÷ 120 × 5 = 11.25 mL. Estimate: about twice 120 mg, so about twice 5 mL.

whyNot.0: Decimal slip: ten times too much.
whyNot.2: Decimal slip: ten times too little.

C.q: An infusion of 1000 mL is running at 125 mL per hour. How many hours will it take to finish?
C.why: Time = volume ÷ rate = 1000 ÷ 125 = 8 hours. Estimate: 125 is one-eighth of 1000.

whyNot.1: Decimal slip: ten times too long.
whyNot.3: Decimal slip: ten times too short.

reteach.title: Guess, then check the guess
reteach.question: 400 mg is prescribed from 200 mg/5 mL. Roughly how much should it be?

blocks.h: Twice the strength, twice the volume
blocks.body: 400 mg is twice 200 mg, so the volume is twice 5 mL: 10 mL. If your calculator says 2.5 mL or 100 mL, something has slipped.

blocks.text: 2.5 mL is the upside-down fraction (200 ÷ 400 × 5); it is smaller than the stock volume even though you want more than the stock strength.

explain.body: Wanting more than the stock strength means more than the stock volume.

test.q: You have a prescription for 400 mg. The bottle label reads 200 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Inverted; you want more than 200 mg, so more than 5 mL.
whyNot.1: Decimal slip: ten times too little.
whyNot.2: Decimal slip: ten times too much.

explain.body: 0.25 g is 250 mg: compare like with like.

test.q: You have a prescription for 0.25 g. The tablets contain 125 mg each. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.0: Did not convert g to mg.
whyNot.2: Decimal slip: ten times too many.

explain.body: One injection is usually 0.1 to 5 mL in Part A items.

test.q: You have a prescription for 75 mg. The ampoule label reads 50 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Decimal slip: 15 mL is far too much for one injection.
whyNot.3: Decimal slip: ten times too little.

explain.body: Pump rates in Part A are usually 5 to 500 mL per hour.

test.q: Prescription: 5% glucose, 500 mL, IV, over 4 hours. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?

whyNot.1: Decimal slip: ten times too slow.
